title: Treat those below you
hookLine: treat those beneath you as you'd want to be treated by those above (Letters 47)

lines: THE WHOLE ADVICE IN ONE SENTENCE.
cards: Watch how someone talks to their boss. Then watch the same person talk to a new intern, a cleaner, a delivery driver who's running late.
The gap between those two voices tells you more about a person than almost anything they say about themselves. Everyone has someone above them and someone below, in some room, on some day.
In the middle of the forty-seventh letter, Seneca pauses: if you want the whole of my advice in one sentence, here it is.

teach.h: AS YOU'D BE TREATED FROM ABOVE.
teach.b: Live with someone beneath you the way you'd want someone above you to live with you. That, he says, is the heart of his teaching.
Whenever you remember how much power you have over another person, remember that someone has just as much power over you.
Fortune can swap the places. He reminds Lucilius of the Roman army destroyed in Germany under the general Varus.
Men of high birth, who'd hoped to climb into the Senate, ended up enslaved, one herding sheep, another guarding a hut. Then a sharper question. Is he a slave?

teach.h: SHOW ME SOMEONE WHO ISN'T A SLAVE.
teach.b: Show me someone who isn't. One is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and all of us to hope and to fear. The one serving may be freer inside than the one being served.
Last, a master should want to be respected rather than feared.
Fear makes enemies; respect can make something close to friendship. Other paths have their own form of this rule; Seneca's has a particular angle.
It's aimed at whoever holds the power right now, which on some days is you.

how: Readers of Seneca sometimes check how they speak to people with less power than they have, asking whether they'd accept the same tone from someone above them.

o: a Roman senator who freed all of his own slaves
the general whose lost army sent noblemen into slavery
an emperor remembered for cruelty to his servants

games.q: above and below — tap the pairs.
p: treat below as you'd be treated

s: Seneca says a master should want to be feared
he says respected rather than feared; fear makes enemies.
Seneca points to men of high birth enslaved after Varus' defeat
fortune made one a shepherd and another a hut-keeper.
Seneca thought only enslaved people could be called slaves
he says one is a slave to lust, another to greed, all to hope and fear.

games.q: you run a small team, and a new hire makes the same mistake twice. what does the forty-seventh letter ask?
o: make them fear the next mistake.
speak to them as you'd want your own boss to speak to you.
games.why: Seneca's whole advice: live with those beneath you as you'd want those above to live with you.

practice: Think of one place where you have a little power over someone, a child, a junior colleague, a younger sibling, a pet even, and picture the last time you spoke to them.
Now picture the person with power over you speaking to you in exactly that tone, and notice how it feels. Breathe, and imagine one small change in how you'll speak next time.

wordCard.voice: Varus. The Roman general whose army's defeat shows how fortune can swap the places of those above and those below. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 47.11: live with one beneath you in this way (as you'd want one above you to live with you).

carryVoice: Your line: as I'd be treated. Power over someone is a place fortune can swap. Day four hundred sixty-three.
